title: A king who knew not Joseph (Exodus 1:8–14)
hookLine: a new Pharaoh, fear of a growing people, and slavery

cards: The second book of the Torah opens with a list of names: Jacob's sons who came down to Egypt, seventy people. That's why it's called Shemot, Names. Then Joseph dies, and all his brothers, and that whole generation.

Their children have children, and the text piles up the words: they were fruitful, they swarmed, they multiplied, they grew very strong, and the land was filled with them. A family has become a people.
Then one short verse turns everything: "Now there arose a new king over Egypt, who knew not Joseph."

teach.h: A NEW KING, OR ONE WHO CHOSE TO FORGET?
teach.b: Who knew not Joseph. How could a Pharaoh not know the man who saved Egypt from famine? The Talmud records two answers.
One rabbi says it really was a new king. The other says it was the same king, who made new decrees, and acted as if he'd never known Joseph. Forgetting on purpose.

teach.h: TOO MANY AND TOO MIGHTY FOR US.
teach.b: The children of Israel are too many and too mighty for us.

teach.h: LET US DEAL WISELY WITH THEM.
teach.b: "Come, let us deal wisely with them," in case there's a war, and they join our enemies. Nobody has done anything. There's no crime, no rebellion.
Only a number, and a fear of what that number might do someday. From fear comes a plan: taskmasters and forced labor, building the store cities of Pithom and Raamses.

teach.h: THE MORE THEY AFFLICTED, THE MORE THEY GREW.
teach.b: Then the Torah says something almost defiant: "But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied."
The Egyptians came to dread them, so the labor gets harder: mortar, brick, work in the fields, all of it made bitter. This is how the story of the Exodus begins. Not with a monster.
With a man who forgot what someone had done for his country, looked at a group of neighbors, and saw a threat.
Jews retell this story every year at the Passover seder, and some teachers point out how ordinary its first step is. Forgetting.
Then fear. Then cruelty that feels, to the people doing it, like being wise.

how: The book of Exodus, Shemot in Hebrew, begins its synagogue reading each winter, and its story of slavery and freedom is retold at the Passover seder every spring.

o: Names: the Hebrew title of the book of Exodus
Exodus: the Hebrew word for leaving Egypt
Slaves: what the new Pharaoh called Israel

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: the Israelites had rebelled against Egypt
nobody had done anything. Pharaoh feared what they might do.
the rabbis debated whether the king was really new
one said new; another said the same king, acting as if he never knew Joseph.
the harder the labor, the fewer the Israelites became
"the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied."

games.q: you're Pharaoh's advisor. a foreign people in your land is growing fast. they've done nothing wrong. Pharaoh asks what to do.
o: welcome them; their ancestor saved Egypt.
deal wisely with them before they grow stronger.
games.why: Pharaoh chooses "come, let us deal wisely with them": taskmasters, forced labor, and slavery. fear, dressed up as wisdom.

practice: Think of the last time you heard a group of people talked about as a threat: too many of them, they'll take over. Maybe it was on the news; maybe you've thought it.
Ask what the fear was based on, something they did or something someone imagined they might do, and just see the first step.
